Conceptual overview: the living review pipeline

Source: vignettes/conceptual_overview.Rmd
conceptual_overview.Rmd

Systematic reviews go out of date quickly. A living review is updated as new evidence appears. Two R packages work together to make that practical:

  • metawoRld owns the review: settings, screening criteria, the schema describing what is extracted, the validated study data, and the website. It has no AI dependencies and can be used on its own with manual data entry.
  • DataFindR uses large language models (through ellmer) to screen studies and extract data into a metawoRld project.

DataFindR depends on metawoRld, never the other way around.

The project

create_metawoRld() creates a folder (by default a Git repository):

my_review/
├── _metawoRld.yml           # name, description, inclusion/exclusion criteria
├── _extraction_schema.yml   # what is extracted from each study
├── _assessment_schema.yml   # what a screening decision looks like
├── _extraction_prompt.txt   # LLM instructions (used by DataFindR)
├── _assessment_prompt.txt
├── data/
│   └── <study id>/
│       ├── metadata.yml     # design, population, methods, groups
│       └── data.csv         # one row per reported statistic
├── .metawoRld_cache/        # DataFindR's cached LLM results (shareable)
└── index.qmd, studies.qmd, data.qmd, _quarto.yml, ...   # website

Studies are stored under their DOI or PMID (normalized, and encoded for the file system with sanitize_id()), so cached screening/extraction results and stored data always refer to the same paper.

The schema

The templates are generic: studies have methods and groups, and every reported statistic is a data point with a method_id, group_id, variable_name, timepoint, sample_size, statistic_type and up to three values. Edit _extraction_schema.yml to fit your review: add fields, tighten descriptions, or turn free-text fields into enums.

A schema node looks like this:

group_id:
  _type: string                 # object, array, string, integer, number, boolean, enum
  _description: "Shown to the LLM."
  _required: true               # default
  _ref: groups.group_id         # must match an id in metadata$groups

_ref links are checked by validate_links() and used by load_metawoRld() to join, for example, group_name and method_unit onto the data.

Pipeline

  1. Set up the project with create_metawoRld() and adjust the schema and criteria.
  2. Identify records: DataFindR::df_search_pubmed() (repeat it to pick up new publications), or df_fetch_metadata() / df_add_metadata().
  3. Screen titles and abstracts: DataFindR::df_assess_batch() in parallel or with discounted batch APIs; review and override in df_shiny_assess().
  4. Extract data from full texts of included studies: DataFindR::df_extract_batch(); check and correct in df_shiny_extract().
  5. Import: DataFindR::df_import_batch() validates each study with add_study_data() and stores it.
  6. Check with validate_world(), follow progress with DataFindR::df_status() and df_prisma_counts().
  7. Publish with generate_website(); use_github_action_quarto() makes GitHub rebuild the site on every push.
  8. Analyse with load_metawoRld().

Every LLM result is cached in the project together with the model, token use, cost and a fingerprint of the prompt, schema and criteria. Re-running a step only processes new studies or studies whose results were produced with an outdated setup. Manual decisions and corrections are never overwritten.

Without AI

All metawoRld functions work without DataFindR. add_study_template() writes placeholder files for manual entry and validate_study() checks them.
